tagline: A UNESCO World Heritage capital and Brazil's colonial launch-town face each other across the Baía de São Marcos — 1.8 million ferry passengers a year at the record, and a tide so big it decides when the boats may sail.
summary: São Luís, the azulejo-tiled UNESCO World Heritage capital of Maranhão, is separated from Alcântara — a perfectly preserved colonial town that now hosts Brazil's equatorial space center — by roughly ten nautical miles of the Baía de São Marcos. The water is already the main road: car ferries out of Ponta da Espera carried 1.8 million passengers in their record year, and open launches leave the historic Cais da Praia Grande for Alcântara whenever the seven-meter tide allows. That tide is the whole story — departures shift daily, festival queues stretch past four hours, and the state is building a new deep-water pier just to escape it. A foiling-electric layer flies above the bay's chop, draws only 1.5 feet at the dock, and turns a tide-hostage 90-minute crossing into a reliable 25-minute flight between two of Brazil's most atmospheric waterfronts.

demand_signals.label: Ferry system record
demand_signals.value: 1.8 million passengers + 371,500 vehicles in 2017 through the Ponta da Espera and Cujupe terminals
demand_signals.note: The record year for the São Luís–Alcântara (Cujupe) crossing — an adopted water-commuting habit, not demand to be created
demand_signals.source: Gov. do Maranhão / EMAP (Porto do Itaqui press office)

demand_signals.label: Carnival peak load
demand_signals.value: 71,737 passengers + 14,300 vehicles in 11 days (Feb 12–22, 2026), with 15 extra sailings; 71,461 passengers in the same 2025 window
demand_signals.note: EMAP suspended advance ticket sales on peak days just to manage the crush — capacity, not demand, is the constraint

demand_signals.label: São Luís tourism record
demand_signals.value: 3 million visitors in 2024, with hotel occupancy peaking at 82% in July
demand_signals.note: The UNESCO historic center and the Bumba Meu Boi festival season (itself UNESCO intangible heritage) drive a strong June–July peak — exactly when ferry queues are worst
demand_signals.source: Secretaria Municipal de Turismo de São Luís (via Brasilturis, Apr 2025)

demand_signals.label: Hinterland served
demand_signals.value: The crossing is the short link for ~35 municipalities and ~2.5 million residents of the Baixada Maranhense, cutting up to 350 km of road
demand_signals.note: Four licensed operators run a six-vessel ferry fleet on 12 scheduled round trips a day — up to 20 on holidays
demand_signals.source: EMAP / Travessia São Luís–Alcântara (Wikipedia, citing state documents)

demand_signals.label: Alcântara space corridor
demand_signals.value: ~20 commercial contracts under negotiation for launches from the Centro Espacial de Alcântara; first non-government launch campaigns in preparation
demand_signals.note: Launch-campaign crews, agencies and VIP visitors all funnel through a town reachable fastest by water from São Luís

demand_signals.label: The tide gate
demand_signals.value: Tidal range in the Baía de São Marcos exceeds 7 m on equinoctial springs — among the largest in Brazil
demand_signals.note: Today's Alcântara launches depart 'conforme a maré': the schedule moves every day and the Praia Grande quay dries out. A 1.5-ft-draft foiling shuttle widens the operating window dramatically
demand_signals.source: Baías do Brasil / COPPE-UFRJ; Marinha do Brasil tidal-current charts

use_cases.title: Tide-proof Alcântara express
use_cases.body: A scheduled foiling shuttle from the Cais da Praia Grande (and the planned Ponta d'Areia pier) to Alcântara's Terminal Hidroviário — flying above the bay chop in ~25 minutes, with shallow 1.5-ft draft stretching the tidal operating window that today dictates the whole timetable.

use_cases.title: UNESCO-to-colonial heritage hop
use_cases.body: São Luís sells the day trip to Alcântara to virtually every visitor — 3 million came in 2024. A silent electric crossing between two historic waterfronts becomes an attraction in itself, replacing diesel launches at the door of a World Heritage center.

use_cases.title: Space-center crew and VIP runs
use_cases.body: Launch campaigns at the Centro Espacial de Alcântara bring engineers, agencies and delegations who today face a tide-dependent boat or a 3–4 hour road loop. A guaranteed-schedule foiling run from São Luís puts the launch town 25 minutes from the capital's hotels.

use_cases.title: Festival surge relief
use_cases.body: Carnival and São João push the ferry system past its limits — 71,737 passengers in 11 days of Carnival 2026, queues over four hours at peaks. High-frequency foot-passenger foiling shuttles between Ponta da Espera and Cujupe peel commuters and festival-goers out of the vehicle-ferry queue.

journeys.from: Cais da Praia Grande (São Luís historic center)
journeys.to: Terminal Hidroviário de Alcântara (Porto do Jacaré)
journeys.today: An open lancha or catamaran, R$20 a leg, 1h15–1h45 across a choppy bay — and it only sails when the seven-meter tide allows, so the timetable changes every day.
journeys.with_navier: A ~25-minute foiling flight above the chop, on a fixed schedule the tide can't dictate — shallow 1.5-ft draft keeps the historic quay usable far longer each day.

journeys.from: Terminal da Ponta da Espera (São Luís)
journeys.today: A 1.5-hour vehicle-ferry crossing; at Carnival and São João the queue for a place stretches past four hours and advance sales get suspended.
journeys.with_navier: A ~20-minute foot-passenger express alongside the car ferry, absorbing the surge and giving the Baixada's 2.5 million residents a fast option.

journeys.from: Espigão Costeiro da Ponta d'Areia (São Luís hotel district)
journeys.today: No service — the state is studying a new deep-water pier at the Espigão precisely because the Praia Grande quay dries out at low tide.
journeys.with_navier: A foiling shuttle from the beach-hotel district that needs no dredging and no deep-water berth — the boarding point the project imagines, served by a vessel that already fits it.

journeys.from: Iate Clube / Marina Ilha Boat (Ponta d'Areia)
journeys.to: Alcântara & the Baía de São Marcos
journeys.today: Private speedboats pound across short, steep bay chop raised by strong trade winds over shallow water.
journeys.with_navier: A silent foiling day-charter — heritage waterfront, mangrove coast and launch-town views with no pounding and no wake.

journeys.to: Cais de São José de Ribamar
journeys.today: A road trip across the island; the pilgrimage town's own bay (Baía de São José) has no scheduled water link to the capital's waterfront.
journeys.with_navier: A coastal foiling run around the island's beach coast — Ponta d'Areia, Calhau, Araçagi — linking the two bays; the sea path wraps the island's northern headlands (~28 nm vs ~15 nm straight-line).

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The entire core network sits inside a ~13 nm radius — Praia Grande↔Alcântara (~10 nm), Ponta da Espera↔Cujupe (~10 nm), Ponta d'Areia↔Alcântara (~9 nm) — trivial for the 70 nm all-electric envelope with charging at the São Luís marinas and terminals. Foiling above the wind-chop and a 1.5-ft draft directly answer this market's two operational curses: rough shallow water and a 7 m tide.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Quanta-LR's 700 nm hybrid range opens the long coastal legs with no charging-infrastructure dependency: east past São José de Ribamar toward Icatu and the Lençóis Maranhenses gateway at Barreirinhas (the state's own planned ferry corridor), and west along the Reentrâncias Maranhenses mangrove coast toward Belém — turning São Luís into the hub of a northern-coast network.

competitive_landscape: The water is already the main road, run today by four licensed ferry operators — Serviporto, Internacional Marítima, Henvil and Banav — with a six-vessel fleet on 12 scheduled round trips a day between Ponta da Espera and Cujupe, plus lancha and catamaran operators (e.g. Lancha Bahia Star, R$20 a leg) out of the Cais da Praia Grande. Demand routinely outruns supply: 71,737 passengers crossed in 11 days of Carnival 2026, festival queues exceed four hours, breakdowns of the ageing diesel fleet make local news, and lancha departures remain hostage to the tide. That is strong, proven demand for exactly the reliability and speed a foiling-electric layer adds on top of the incumbent system.
seasonality: Equatorial and warm year-round. The rainy season runs roughly January–June (heaviest March–May); July–December is dry with strong, steady easterly trade winds that raise short chop on the shallow bay — the sea state foiling glides above. The structural rhythm is tidal, not seasonal: spring tides beyond 7 m gate today's lancha timetable daily, and floating pontoons plus a 1.5-ft draft are the design answer. Demand peaks at Carnival (February) and the two-month São João / Bumba Meu Boi season (June–July), when São Luís hotel occupancy hits its 82% record. No cyclone exposure.
regulatory_note: EMAP (Empresa Maranhense de Administração Portuária), the state port company, administers both ferry terminals and — under state law 11.909/2023 — plans, concedes, regulates and inspects intermunicipal waterway passenger transport, taking over from MOB (Agência Estadual de Mobilidade Urbana e Serviços Públicos), which still runs mobility integration and ticketing programs and opened the new Terminal de Passageiros da Baixada in September 2025. The Brazilian Navy's Capitania dos Portos do Maranhão (CP-MA) certifies vessels and crews. Both waterfronts carry heritage regimes — São Luís's historic center is UNESCO World Heritage and Alcântara is a national monument under IPHAN — which reward a silent, zero-emission, low-wake arrival at the historic quays.
signature_routes: Cais da Praia Grande ↔ Alcântara / Porto do Jacaré (the heritage crossing, freed from the tide)
Ponta da Espera ↔ Cujupe (foot-passenger express over Brazil's festival-surge ferry corridor)
Espigão Costeiro da Ponta d'Areia ↔ Alcântara (the state's own planned deep-water pier, served without dredging)
São Luís ↔ São José de Ribamar → Icatu (the planned Lençóis Maranhenses gateway corridor)

precedents.why_it_matters: Demonstrates electric foiling as the backbone of scheduled inter-island mobility at national scale — the playbook for making a foiling fleet the transport layer of a bay-and-islands region, not a novelty.

precedents.what: State pier project at the Espigão Costeiro da Ponta d'Areia
precedents.why_it_matters: The state has already identified the core problem — tide-gated departures from the shallow Praia Grande quay — and is planning infrastructure to fix it. A 1.5-ft-draft foiling shuttle delivers the same outcome with far lighter infrastructure, at the pier the project envisions.
